NPU Compilation Optimization

What dominates Intel NPU-5 compile time, why, and what to fix — 120 cold configs over 5 architecture families (Gemma-2, TinyLlama, Llama-3.2, Phi-3, Qwen2), sizes 0.5–7.6 B, prompt window 128 → 32768, three weight precisions (int4 / int8 / fp16), 10 cold repeats each (OpenVINO 2026.0).

The dominant pass is not fixed by architecture — it's set by how big the compile is. Every family walks the same path: tiling-search → memory-scheduling → serialization. And each pass's cost tracks the IR/schedule size it processes — which is the handle to fix it.

4 · Same fingerprint, different architectures

5 · Precision: a two-way tug-of-war, not "fewer bits = faster"

Compile cost is a tug-of-war between two effects. The dequantization / weight-table machinery that int8 and int4 bolt on penalises the quantized formats — so for small-to-mid models fp16 compiles fastest (≈0.58× int8) despite its larger weights. But fp16 also carries 2× the weight bytes, and by 7 B that weight-DMA volume takes over: fp16 flips to ≈1.88× int8 (up to 2.4× at mid windows). int4 wins both ways — it has the dequant machinery but half the bytes — staying ≤0.99× int8 at every size. The mechanism shows in the pipeline: the quantized formats (int4, int8) land their heaviest work in the serialization back-end (the weight tables they serialize), while fp16 stays tiling-search-dominated.

6 · Convolutional graphs — same structure, different passes

The pattern generalises across modality, with a twist. Across 31 CNN configs (7 families — ResNet-18→152 swept 128→640 px, plus EfficientNet, MobileNetV3, DenseNet, RegNet, Inception, ConvNeXt), FeasibleAllocation never dominates a single compile (0/31). Conv graphs are tiling + vertical-fusion bound: MultiClusterStrategy (tiling) leads at low resolution and hands off to MergeVfSubgraphs (vertical fusion) as resolution grows. Same workload-gated shape as the LLMs — attention graphs escalate into scheduling/serialization; conv graphs escalate into tiling/fusion.

7 · Testing a lever: what happens if the compiler stops prefetching

The levers above are hypotheses until one is measured. prefetching is a single pipeline option gating both the prefetch tiling search and the FeasibleAllocation prefetch scheduler, so it is the one lever that can be switched with a property rather than a patch: NPU_COMPILATION_MODE_PARAMS="prefetching=false". Two arms per cell, compiled back-to-back, then inferred in the same process so the latency belongs to the blob whose compile was just timed.

The compile saving is large and unconditional — 13–54% (up to 227s off a single 7B compile). The inference cost is not: its sign flips with model size. 0.5B, 1.8B pay for it; 3.1B, 7.6B get faster decode as well — up to 15% per token. For prefill the flip has a threshold: prefetching only starts paying once the window is long enough to hold compute to hide movement behind (3.1B at W=1024, 7.6B at W=4096) — and that threshold rises with model size.

Where the compile saving actually comes from

Mostly not from one pass. Below 7.6B no single pass accounts for more than 6% of the saving — it is spread across nearly the whole pipeline, and per-pass timings account for 94–97% of the wall-clock saving, so this is not unmeasured overhead. The exception is 7.6B, where FeasibleAllocation alone gives back 286s (23%) — that is the CMX scheduler falling out of the regime §3 identifies. Tiling search, the other thing the flag gates, is never more than 6%.

The reason nearly every pass gets cheaper at once is visible in the last column: the pipeline is identical (3794 pass invocations either way) but the schedule it processes is 25–49% smaller. Prefetching does not move more data — it splits the same work into many more, smaller tasks so they can be issued early. Every downstream pass then walks a bigger task graph.

Why decode gets faster on the big models

Not because less data moves. On the decode graph — the one re-executed for every generated token — the work is almost unchanged when prefetching is off: DMA work -3 to -7% and DPU work about −7%. What collapses is the number of scheduled tasks. Prefetching splits the same transfers into many more, smaller ones so they can be issued early, and removing it cuts the decode task graph by 39–54% at 3.1B/7.6B against only 18–19% at 0.5B/1.8B. Every task carries fixed cost the cycle model never charges for — barrier programming, descriptor fetch, DMA setup — so the big models shed enough per-task overhead to more than pay back the lost overlap, and the small models do not. That is the sign flip.

The compiler's own model gets it backwards: it predicts decode should get slower by about +1.9% for every size. It is right in sign for 0.5B/1.8B and wrong for 3.1B/7.6B, because it prices work and overlap but not the cost of having more tasks to run.

Control — is the big-model speedup an artifact?

A result that says "do less scheduling, go faster" deserves suspicion, so the sweep's design was attacked directly. In the sweep, prefetch-on always compiled first inside a cell and each arm was measured in its own process, so a warmed device or thermal drift could have produced the gap. The control removes both: it compiles both arms in one process with the order reversed (off first), then measures decode by alternating between them over six rounds, alternating which arm leads each round. It also compares the two blobs' prefill logits on identical input — a blob that is faster because it computes something different would be a bug, not a speedup.

modelwindowdecode, prefetch ondecode, prefetch off deltaworst spreadoutput vs the other arm
3.1BW=20481,381 ms1,238 ms-10.4%3 msbit-identical
7.6BW=20483,072 ms2,624 ms-14.6%40 msbit-identical

The gap survives unchanged — the control reproduces the sweep to within a few tenths of a percent — and where the logits were compared the two arms are bit-identical. The effect is neither an ordering artifact nor a correctness regression.

Read this narrowly. prefetching is global — it gates the tiling search as well as the allocator, so this is the prefetch feature, not the allocator in isolation; separating them would need a patched compiler. The overlap/DMA-work numbers are the compiler's modelled schedule, not hardware counters: per-op runtime profiling is unavailable through NPUW (get_profiling_info() returns empty), which is itself part of the finding — the only per-op view available is the model that turns out to mispredict. 4 of 36 cells (0.5B@W=128, 0.5B@W=512, 0.5B@W=4096, 0.5B@W=8192) are unresolved — their arm-to-arm decode difference is smaller than the spread within an arm (up to 20.8 ms on a ~130 ms decode), so they carry no direction and are excluded from the decode ranges quoted here. All four are 0.5B: the smallest model is the one whose decode effect is the same size as its run-to-run noise.

8 · The fixable pattern → what to optimize

Because cost is driven by IR/schedule size in a known regime, the levers are direct:

regime (when)dominant passroot causefix
every compile—recompiling from scratch Warm blob cache — a recompile is 20–30× a blob-load. Biggest, universal win.
small / short (≤3B)MultiClusterStrategy serial tiling search (user/wall≈1.0) Cache / reuse strategy_out.json across shapes; lower search effort.
7B, mid windowFeasibleAllocation #tasks explodes → greedy simulate-and-spill re-run 2–3× Fewer/larger tiles (cut #tasks); bound the window; ship precompiled ELF.
≥3B, any windowMultiClusterStrategy
+ FeasibleAllocation		 prefetch tiling + prefetch scheduling search Turn prefetching off (prefetching=false) — measured in §7: 53% off the compile at best and 9–14% faster decode at 3B/7B. Below 3B it costs latency; above it, it is free both ways.
extreme window (≥16K)ELF serialization artifact size grows linearly with W Precompiled-blob shipping; the materialization is mechanical, don't repeat it.

Method: Intel Core Ultra 7 356H, NPU 5 (intel_vpu), OpenVINO 2026.0, driver-compiler 1.33. Weights swept at int4 (symmetric, group-128), int8 and fp16 — each export's on-disk element types verified (fp16 defeats the optimum silent-int8 trap; int4 uses --sym to dodge a group-quant location-verifier compiler bug that fails asymmetric int4). Fully-cold compiles (NPU_BYPASS_UMD_CACHING, isolated subprocess per repeat), NPUW_LLM window sweep. Per-pass time = the VPUX compiler's MLIR PassTiming (wall, inclusive of analyses, pipeline groups excluded); mean over 10 repeats (4 at W≥8192). Why-costly metrics from the release compiler's own instrumentation via NPU_COMPILATION_MODE_PARAMS (enable-schedule-trace, write-strategy-to-json) + built-in dump-statistics-of-ie-ops. The §3 FeasibleAllocation-knee figure is measured on a from-source build of the open npu_compiler (compiler-in-plugin, commit 30d2bb8, OpenVINO 2026.2) — the same MLIR passes run in-process on the schedulable compiler, cold, 2 repeats, window 128→32768. Sparse-MoE (Granite) and hybrid-SSM (Qwen3.5) do not compile on NPU 5 (dynamic shapes). CNNs exported via optimum --library timm, reshaped to static NCHW; input resolution is the plain-static workload axis. vgg16 excluded — its 102M-param fc1 fails SplitNCEOpsOntoWorkloads on NPU 5. Ungated model mirrors; no HF token.
